messages.content: I need to split identifiers like 'HTTPServerError' and 'parseXMLDoc' into their words for a search index. Splitting before every capital letter mangles the acronyms ('H', 'T', 'T', 'P', ...). How do I do it with regex?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
camelCase -> ['camel', 'Case']
PascalCase -> ['Pascal', 'Case']
HTTPServerError -> ['HTTP', 'Server', 'Error']
parseXMLDoc -> ['parse', 'XML', 'Doc']
version2Beta -> ['version2', 'Beta']
already -> ['already']

The trick is that re.split can split on zero-width positions, so the pattern never consumes any letters — it just names the places where a cut is legal. Two rules cover the cases. First, `(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])`: a boundary between a lowercase letter or digit and an uppercase letter, the ordinary camelCase seam — that's what splits 'camel|Case' and 'version2|Beta'. Second, `(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])`: a boundary inside a capital run, just before its LAST capital, when that capital starts a normal capitalized word. In 'HTTPServerError' the run is 'HTTPS' followed by 'erver', so the cut lands before the 'S' of 'Server', giving 'HTTP' intact instead of confetti. The output shows both rules cooperating: 'parseXMLDoc' becomes ['parse', 'XML', 'Doc']. Notice both rules are pure lookaround — lookbehind checks what kind of character precedes the cut, lookahead checks what follows. That's the general shape of lookaround work: the match is a position, and the assertions are its context.
When should I use a lookahead instead of just capturing a group and checking it in code afterwards?

Use a lookahead when the surrounding text is a CONDITION on the match, not data you need. 'Find amounts, but only when followed by the word "total"' — the word 'total' is evidence, not payload, so `\d+(?= total)` keeps it out of the match and out of your results. Capture a group instead when you need the context's VALUE (to store it, transform it, or report it), or when the condition needs real logic a pattern can't express — 'the next number must be larger than this one', 'the prefix must be one of these 400 codes', anything with arithmetic or a lookup table. Two more signals: if the assertion makes the pattern hard to read, moving the check into code usually wins, because code checks can be named, logged, and unit-tested individually. And if the same condition applies to many patterns, a code filter applied to results is written once, while a lookahead has to be pasted into every pattern. Lookarounds are for local, textual, throwaway conditions; groups and code are for everything else.

From invoice text like 'The invoice lists $42 for parts, 17 bolts, a fee of $8, and 3 hours of labor at $19.99 each, plus 2 clamps', I want only the numbers that are NOT prices — the counts. I tried a negative lookbehind for the dollar sign and the results are wrong in a weird way. What's happening?

arguments.code:
import re

text = ('The invoice lists $42 for parts, 17 bolts, a fee of $8, and 3 hours '
        'of labor at $19.99 each, plus 2 clamps.')

naive = re.findall(r'(?<!\$)\d+', text)
print('naive (?<!$) only     :', naive)

# an optional space inside a lookbehind makes its width variable, which
# re rejects - so the two guards are stacked as separate lookbehinds:
# not preceded by a digit/dot/$ right here, and not preceded by "$ "
fixed = re.findall(r'(?<!\$ )(?<![\d$.])\d+(?:\.\d+)?', text)
print('fixed (stacked guards):', fixed)

messages.content: Your lookbehind guards only the position where a match STARTS, and findall retries at every position. Look at the naive output: ['2', '17', '3', '9', '99', '2']. The '2' leaked out of '$42' — the '4' is blocked because it directly follows '$', but then the engine slides one character right and tries to start the match at '2', where the character before is '4', the guard passes, and '\d+' happily matches. '$19.99' leaks twice: a '9' from the middle and the '99' after the decimal point. The fix is to guard against every way a match could start INSIDE a number or a price: not preceded by a digit, a dot, or a '$'. One subtlety the first version of this fix hit: you can't write the guard as `(?<![\d$.] ?)` with an optional space, because an optional element makes the lookbehind's width variable and Python rejects it outright. Stacking two fixed-width lookbehinds — `(?<!\$ )` for the '$ 42' shape and `(?<![\d$.])` for the immediate neighbour — expresses the same idea legally. Result: ['17', '3', '2'], exactly the counts.

I want to extract surnames after titles — 'Dr. Patel', 'Mr. Chen', 'Ms. Rivera', 'Prof. Osei' — using a lookbehind so the title isn't part of the match. Python keeps rejecting my pattern. Why, and what's the workaround?

arguments.code:
import re

text = 'Dr. Patel arrived. Mr. Chen left. Ms. Rivera stayed. Prof. Osei spoke.'

same_width = re.compile(r'(?<=(?:Dr|Mr|Ms)\. )(\w+)')
print('same-width titles:', same_width.findall(text))

try:
    re.compile(r'(?<=(?:Dr|Mr|Ms|Prof)\. )(\w+)')
    print('mixed widths: compiled')
except re.error as e:
    print('mixed widths: re.error:', e)

# workaround: one lookbehind per width, combined as alternation branches
either = re.compile(r'(?:(?<=(?:Dr|Mr|Ms)\. )|(?<=Prof\. ))(\w+)')
print('two lookbehinds  :', either.findall(text))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
same-width titles: ['Patel', 'Chen', 'Rivera']
mixed widths: re.error: look-behind requires fixed-width pattern
two lookbehinds  : ['Patel', 'Chen', 'Rivera', 'Osei']

Python's re requires a lookbehind to have ONE fixed width for the whole assertion — the engine needs to know exactly how many characters to step back. Alternation is fine as long as every branch has the SAME width: 'Dr. ', 'Mr. ' and 'Ms. ' are all 4 characters, so `(?<=(?:Dr|Mr|Ms)\. )` compiles and extracts Patel, Chen and Rivera. Adding 'Prof' makes the branches 4 or 6 wide, and compilation dies with 'look-behind requires fixed-width pattern' — even though each individual branch is fixed-width. (The third-party regex module relaxes this; stdlib re does not.) The workaround shown is one lookbehind per width, joined by alternation at the top level: `(?:(?<=(?:Dr|Mr|Ms)\. )|(?<=Prof\. ))(\w+)`. Each branch of the outer alternation carries its own legal lookbehind, and all four names come out. The other standard workaround is to stop fighting for a lookbehind: capture the title in a group, `(Dr\.|Mr\.|Ms\.|Prof\.)\s+(\w+)`, and read group 2.
My lookbehind works, but a coworker says I should just capture the prefix in a group and ignore group 1. When is she right?

She's right more often than lookbehind fans admit. Capturing the prefix — `(Dr\.|Prof\.)\s+(\w+)` and reading group 2 — has real advantages: the prefix can be any length (no fixed-width rule), the pattern ports to engines with weak or no lookbehind support, and when the prefix turns out to matter later ('wait, we also need the title'), it's already captured instead of asserted away. The lookbehind earns its complexity in narrower situations: when you need findall to return ONLY the target strings (with a group, findall returns tuples and you post-process), when the match position itself is the product — re.split cut points, re.sub insertion points, highlighter spans — and when the same target pattern is reused in several contexts with different prefixes. A good default: reach for the capture group first; switch to a lookbehind when you can name the specific thing the group version makes awkward.

arguments.code:
import re

text = 'the cat sat; a cat-like robot; wildcat energy; cat2 is a robot name; the CAT slept'

print('plain word boundary :', re.findall(r'\bcat\b', text))
print('token boundary      :', re.findall(r'(?<![\w-])cat(?![\w-])', text))
print('token + ignore case :', re.findall(r'(?<![\w-])cat(?![\w-])', text, re.I))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
plain word boundary : ['cat', 'cat']
token boundary      : ['cat']
token + ignore case : ['cat', 'CAT']

\b has a precise meaning that is only approximately 'word boundary': it's a position where a word character (\w = letters, digits, underscore) meets a non-word character. A hyphen is a non-word character, so in 'cat-like' there IS a \b after 'cat' — the output shows \bcat\b matching both the standalone 'cat' and the 'cat' in 'cat-like'. If your real notion of a token is 'letters glued together by hyphens count as one token', say so explicitly with lookarounds: `(?<![\w-])cat(?![\w-])`. Now the neighbours that disqualify a match are word characters AND hyphens, so 'cat-like' is excluded while the standalone 'cat' survives. Adding re.I brings in 'CAT' as well, giving ['cat', 'CAT']. The general lesson: \b encodes one specific token definition (\w-based). The moment your format's tokens differ — hyphenated words, dotted identifiers, paths — build the boundary out of lookarounds naming exactly the characters that count as 'inside'.
How does the famous thousands-separator one-liner actually work? re.sub(r'\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))', ',', s) looks like magic and I don't trust magic.

It's two assertions about a POSITION, and the substitution inserts a comma at every position that satisfies both. Walk through '1234567'. Candidate positions are the gaps between characters. First assertion, \B: the gap must NOT be a word boundary. Between two digits there's no \w/non-\w transition, so digit-to-digit gaps pass; the gaps at the very start and end of the string are boundaries and are excluded — no leading or trailing comma. Second assertion, the lookahead `(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))`: starting from this gap, the digits ahead must form one or more complete groups of exactly three, and after those groups must come a non-digit (the end of the number). In '1234567' the gap after '1' leaves '234567' = two full groups — comma. The gap after '12' leaves '34567', which is 3+2 — the last group is incomplete, so no comma. The gaps that qualify are exactly the ones a human would pick counting from the right: after '1' and after '1234'. Output confirms: 1000 -> '1,000', 1234567 -> '1,234,567'. The pattern is trustworthy once you see it's not matching digits at all — it's auditing every gap with two questions: 'am I strictly inside the number?' and 'is the rest a whole number of triples?'

Can I combine lookaheads to express 'lines with ERROR but without the word retry'? I tried putting (?!.*retry) right after ERROR in the pattern and it only filters retries that come after the word ERROR.

You diagnosed it exactly: a lookahead is evaluated at the position where it sits in the pattern, and `(?!.*retry)` after `ERROR` only inspects the text from that point forward — a 'retry' earlier in the line is invisible to it. The standard arrangement is to put the negative lookahead at the ANCHOR, before anything is consumed: `^(?!.*retry).*ERROR`. At the start of the line, `(?!.*retry)` scans the whole line and vetoes it if 'retry' appears anywhere; only then does `.*ERROR` go looking for the level. This composes: several lookaheads stacked at the anchor act like a conjunction of whole-line conditions — `^(?!.*retry)(?=.*WARN).*ERROR` demands no 'retry', at least one 'WARN' somewhere, and an 'ERROR'. Think of anchored lookaheads as a WHERE clause evaluated before the match proper begins, and mid-pattern lookaheads as conditions on the remainder only.
I need filenames that contain both 'report' and a 4-digit year, in any order, and never the word 'draft'. Can one pattern do that, or do I filter in code?

One pattern can, using the anchored-lookahead trick three times: `^(?=.*report)(?=.*\d{4})(?!.*draft).*$`. Each lookahead starts from the same position — the beginning of the name — and scans the whole string independently, so order doesn't matter: the first two demand that 'report' and a 4-digit run exist somewhere, the third vetoes any name containing 'draft'. Only if all three assertions pass does the trailing `.*` consume the name as the actual match. This is the idiomatic shape for 'all of these substrings, in any order, minus those' queries. The honest limit: past about three conditions the pattern stops being self-documenting, and a code filter — `if 'report' in name and has_year(name) and 'draft' not in name` — becomes easier to extend, test, and explain. Use the pattern when the condition set is small and stable; graduate to code when it starts growing.

My pattern uses a negative lookbehind to skip amounts with a currency symbol, but it breaks when there's a space after the symbol, like '$ 42'. The lookbehind for just '$' doesn't block it. What are my options?

Three, in increasing order of robustness. First, stack a second lookbehind for the spaced variant: `(?<!\$)(?<!\$ )\d+` — the first blocks '$42', the second blocks '$ 42', because the two characters before the match are '$ '. Stacked lookbehinds are how you say 'not preceded by X and not preceded by Y' when X and Y have different widths; a single lookbehind can't mix widths. Second, allow the optional space inside a CAPTURING approach instead: match the whole amount with an optional symbol group, `(\$\s?)?(\d[\d.]*)`, and decide in code whether group 1 participated — this also survives '€ 42' and 'USD 42' without new lookbehinds. Third, if the text is machine-generated with a fixed set of formats, normalize first (collapse '$ ' to '$') and keep the simple pattern. The lookbehind stack is fine for two variants; when the variants keep multiplying, that's the signal to switch to the capturing approach.

How do I detect a duplicated two-word phrase in prose, like 'the report the report was late'?

A backreference over a two-word group: `\b(\w+\s+\w+)\s+\1\b`. Group 1 captures two words and the whitespace between them; `\1` then demands the identical two words again after a single run of whitespace. It catches 'the report the report' and 'in the in the'. Two practical warnings. First, legitimate English repeats phrases: 'had had', 'that that', 'very very' — a detector should flag candidates for a human, not auto-delete, or it will eventually eat a correct sentence. Second, real-world duplication often differs slightly — punctuation, a line break, different spacing — so `\s+` between the copies matters, and even then a copy with a comma inserted ('the report, the report') slips past. For an editor's lint tool that's an acceptable hit rate; for an automatic rewriter it isn't.

My date reformatter worked until I added an optional group at the front of the pattern — now the substitution produces garbage like '11/2026/'. Nothing else changed. What broke?

arguments.code:
import re

line = '2026-11-26 meeting notes'

v1 = re.compile(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})')
print('v1 numbered :', v1.sub(r'\3/\2/\1', line))

# a teammate adds an optional leading group; every number after it shifts
v2 = re.compile(r'(notes|meeting)? ?(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})')
print('v2 numbered :', v2.sub(r'\3/\2/\1', line))

v2_named = re.compile(r'(?P<kind>notes|meeting)? ?'
                      r'(?P<y>\d{4})-(?P<m>\d{2})-(?P<d>\d{2})')
print('v2 named    :', v2_named.sub(r'\g<d>/\g<m>/\g<y>', line))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
v1 numbered : 26/11/2026 meeting notes
v2 numbered : 11/2026/ meeting notes
v2 named    : 26/11/2026 meeting notes

Your group numbers moved. Group numbers are assigned purely by position — the order of opening parentheses — so inserting `(notes|meeting)?` at the front made it group 1 and shifted the year, month and day to groups 2, 3 and 4. Your replacement string `\3/\2/\1` still refers to the OLD numbering, so it now prints month/year/ plus group 1, which is the optional group that didn't participate and contributes an empty string: '11/2026/'. Nothing raised an error because every reference was still technically valid — the pattern silently rewired itself. The named-group version is immune: groups are called `y`, `m` and `d`, the replacement uses `\g<d>/\g<m>/\g<y>`, and inserting new groups anywhere changes nothing. Rule of thumb: numbered groups are fine inside a pattern you'll never edit again — which is no pattern ever. The moment a pattern has three or more groups or a replacement string, name the groups.
I keep mixing up \1 in the pattern versus \1 in the replacement string. And what does \12 mean?

They're two different languages that happen to share a spelling. In the PATTERN, `\1` is a backreference: 'match the same text group 1 captured' — an instruction to the engine. In the REPLACEMENT string (re.sub's second argument), `\1` is a placeholder: 'insert the text group 1 captured' — no matching happens there at all. The ambiguity: `\12` in a pattern means group 12 if the pattern has 12 groups, otherwise group 1 followed by a literal '2' — context-dependent and unreadable. In a replacement, `\12` has the same problem. The unambiguous spelling is `\g<1>` (and `\g<name>` for named groups): `\g<1>2` always means 'group 1, then a literal 2'. Practical rule: in replacement strings, always use the `\g<>` form; it also survives group insertions when you use names. In patterns, backreferences are rare enough that spelling them `\1` is conventional, but a comment saying which group is meant costs nothing.
When I use re.sub with named groups, how do I reference them in the replacement? And can I mix named and numbered references?

In the replacement string, named groups are `\g<name>`: pattern `(?P<last>\w+), (?P<first>\w+)` with replacement `\g<first> \g<last>` turns 'Doe, Jane' into 'Jane Doe'. You CAN mix — `\g<first>` and `\2` in the same replacement both work — but mixing reintroduces exactly the fragility named groups exist to remove: the numbered references renumber silently when someone edits the pattern, while the named ones don't, so half your replacement rots. Pick names and use them everywhere. For anything more complex than rearranging captured text — case changes, lookups, arithmetic, conditionals — skip the replacement string entirely and pass a FUNCTION to re.sub: it receives the match object, reads `m.group('first')`, and returns whatever string it computes. Function replacements are the maintainable ceiling of re.sub; replacement strings are for pure rearrangement.

The pattern `(\w)\w*\1` under fullmatch says: capture the first letter, allow anything in the middle, and require the last letter to be the same text as the first (the backreference). It sorts the list correctly — level, civic, window, stats, noon and refer pass; banana (b...a) and apple (a...e) fail. The interesting case is 'a', which returns False even though a one-letter word trivially starts and ends with the same letter. What does a backreference do when the group it points to didn't participate in the match — like an optional group that was skipped?

In Python's re, the backreference FAILS — it does not match the empty string. Concretely, `(a)?b\1` against 'b' returns no match: the optional group is skipped, and then `\1` has no captured text to repeat, so that whole match path dies. Against 'aba' it matches, because group 1 captured 'a' and the backreference can repeat it. This surprises people because the group itself, when it doesn't participate, behaves like 'nothing' everywhere else — m.group(1) returns None, findall shows ''. The backreference is stricter: no capture, no match. (Some engines differ — .NET treats it as an empty match — so this is a genuine porting trap.) If you want 'repeat the group if it was there', the pattern has to offer both paths explicitly, typically by putting the group and its backreference inside the same optional unit: `(?:(a)b\1)?b` style restructuring, or simpler, two alternatives. The design lesson: optional groups and backreferences compose badly; if a pattern needs both, test the skipped-group case on purpose, because it will not fail loudly — it will just quietly never match.
I have CSV-ish rows and I need the rows whose first and last fields are identical — like 'ana,widgets,3,ana'. Regex with a backreference, or split?

Both work; split is the better default here. With split it's two obvious operations: `fields = row.split(',')` then `fields[0] == fields[-1]` — readable, and it extends for free when the rule grows ('first equals last AND middle is numeric'). The regex version, `^([^,]+),.*,\1$`, hides two traps: the greedy `.*` in the middle will happily span what you think of as several fields (fine here, but it means the pattern is really saying 'starts with X, ends with X'), and the moment a field can contain a comma — a quoted CSV field — the `[^,]+` premise collapses and you're in real-CSV territory where the csv module is the only correct tool. Use the backreference when the job is purely textual (find rows in a raw file without parsing them, inside an editor, in a grep pipeline). Use split when the fields are data you'll manipulate further. The deciding question is whether you're locating text or processing records.

With named groups `(?P<user>\w+)@(?P<host>[\w.]+)`, a successful fullmatch on 'ana@mint.example' returns {'user': 'ana', 'host': 'mint.example'} — downstream code reads `d['user']` instead of remembering that group 1 was the user. Treat the pattern as an API: named groups are its field names.
I read that atomic groups 'commit' to a match. Show me a case where that changes the RESULT, not just the speed.

arguments.code:
import re

print('plain alternation :', re.search(r'(a|ab)c', 'abc').group(0))
print('atomic group      :', re.search(r'(?>a|ab)c', 'abc'))
print('atomic, reordered :', re.search(r'(?>ab|a)c', 'abc').group(0))
print('atomic, longer    :', re.search(r'(?>a|ab)c', 'ac').group(0))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
plain alternation : abc
atomic group      : None
atomic, reordered : abc
atomic, longer    : ac

Here it is in its smallest form. With a plain group, `(a|ab)c` on 'abc' first tries 'a' for the alternation, then needs 'c' but sees 'b' — so the engine BACKTRACKS, retries the alternation with 'ab', and now 'c' follows: match, 'abc'. Wrap the alternation in an atomic group, `(?>a|ab)c`, and the first choice becomes final: once 'a' matches, the group is sealed. 'c' fails against 'b', and the engine is forbidden from reopening the group to try 'ab' — the whole match returns None. Reordering the branches inside the atomic group to `(?>ab|a)c` flips the result back, because now the committed first choice is the one that works; and on 'ac' the atomic version still matches, since 'a' followed by 'c' was the right commitment all along. So an atomic group is a semantic tool, not only an optimization: it says 'the first way this matches is the only way it may match'. That's exactly right when later alternatives could only produce wrong parses, and exactly wrong when the backtracking was load-bearing.

What are the shapes of evil pattern I should spot in code review, before they spot me in production?

Three shapes cover most real incidents. First, nested quantifiers over the same character class: `(a+)+`, `(\w*)*`, `(.*)*` — an inner run and an outer run free to negotiate how to split the same text. Second, overlapping alternation under a quantifier: `(a|aa)+`, `(\d|\d\d)+`, or alternation branches where one is a prefix of another, repeated — two ways to eat the same character, multiplied by repetition. Third, a quantified group whose body can match empty or can absorb the following token: `^(\w+\s?)*$` is the classic production killer, because `\s?` being optional means spaces can belong to either iteration. All three share the trigger condition: the overall match must FAIL (or come close) on a long input, because success takes the first path and leaves. So the review question is precise: 'show me the longest input on which this pattern almost matches but ultimately fails — how much work does it do there?' If nobody can answer, the pattern doesn't ship. Bonus smell: a pattern that validates with nested quantifiers AND is applied to user-controlled input is a denial-of-service vulnerability with a ticket number waiting to happen.
Why does catastrophic backtracking need the match to FAIL? My evil pattern is fast on all our valid inputs.

Because backtracking is a search for a successful path, and success ends the search. On a valid input, the engine's first greedy choices usually lead straight to a match — for `^(a+)+$` on a clean run of a's, the inner group takes everything, the anchor holds, done, no alternatives explored. The exponential space of groupings only gets ENUMERATED when paths keep failing: the engine tries a grouping, hits the failing tail, backs up, tries the next grouping, and cannot stop until it has proven that none of the 2^(n-1) groupings works. Failure is what converts a lazy search into an exhaustive proof. Two consequences worth internalizing. First, your test suite will never catch this with valid data — you need adversarial, almost-valid inputs (long runs with one wrong character at the end) in the tests. Second, attackers know this: ReDoS payloads are always 'almost valid' strings — a long email-ish prefix with a missing final character — because a wildly invalid string fails fast at the first character and a valid one succeeds fast. The danger zone is the boundary, and it's exactly where fuzzing should aim.

The naive counter recomputes splits(k) from scratch every time any larger problem needs it, and splits(12) needs splits(11), which needs splits(11) again through another path, and so on: the call tree has 2^12 leaves because the same subproblems are solved exponentially many times. Memoization notices that there are only 13 DISTINCT subproblems (n = 0..12), solves each once, and looks up the rest — the answer is identical, the work collapses from exponential to linear. That is, in miniature, the entire trick behind linear-time regex engines: a backtracking engine re-walks the same (pattern position, input position) states over and over, while an automata-based engine tracks the SET of states it's in and visits each state at most once per input character. The states were never exponential — only the paths were. Once you see the partition count and the call count side by side, 'exponential backtracking' stops being a mystery: it's a memoization failure, and the fix — in engines or in your own recursive code — is to stop re-solving identical subproblems.

No — overlap alone is a misdemeanor; it becomes a felony only in combination. Your alternation tries branches left to right at one position: 'Jan' is attempted first and wins on 'January...' too, which may be a CORRECTNESS annoyance (you captured the short form), and worst case the engine tries three branches per position — a small constant factor. (a|aa)+ is dangerous because the overlap sits INSIDE a quantifier: every iteration offers two ways to consume, the choices multiply across iterations, and a failing tail forces the engine to enumerate the product of all those choices. The three ingredients are overlap, repetition, and failure; remove any one and the bomb is defused. Your month pattern has only the first. What you should actually fix in it is branch ORDER and intent: put the longest, most specific branches first ('January' before 'Jan'), or the alternation will keep surprising you by matching less than you expected — a correctness review point, not a security one. Suppose I inherit a suspect pattern I can't rewrite — it's embedded in a vendor config. What runtime defenses do I actually have?

Four layers, roughly in order of ease. Input length caps: backtracking cost is exponential in input length, so a sane maximum (no legitimate email is 10,000 characters) converts an unbounded hang into a bounded one — crude, but it caps the blast radius. Timeouts: Python's re has none built in, so run the match in a worker process or thread pool with a deadline and abandon overdue matches; the third-party regex module is the nicer route — it accepts a `timeout=` argument and raises TimeoutError, a drop-in defense for exactly this situation. Engine swap: for fixed patterns, RE2-backed libraries (google-re2, or Rust's regex via bindings) guarantee linear time, at the price of giving up backreferences and lookarounds — check the vendor pattern doesn't use them. And pre-filtering: a cheap check (length, allowed character set, a simple split-based sanity test) in front of the expensive pattern rejects most garbage before the pattern ever sees it. None of these fix the pattern; they buy you a service that degrades instead of dying while you negotiate the rewrite.

A ratio that stays near 1 per added character means polynomial; a ratio that stays near 2 (or 1.6, or any constant above 1) per character means exponential, and no hardware budget survives it. 'C++' breaks both ends of that definition. At the end: the last '+' is a non-word character and the space after it is also a non-word character, so there is no transition after 'C++' — the \b fails. At the start, if 'C++' follows a space, space-to-'C' IS a transition, so the leading \b passes and the trailing one is the sole killer — which is why the pattern looks 'almost right' in partial tests. The fix is to define the boundary in terms of what YOUR token is made of. If the rule is 'not glued to other letters or digits', use lookarounds: `(?<!\w)C\+\+(?!\w)`. If '+' should also count as inside-the-token (so 'C++17' or 'xC++' are handled per your format's rules), include it: `(?<![\w+])C\+\+(?![\w+])`. Your pattern might be `ERROR\s+(?i:timeout|retry|refused)`: the level must be the literal uppercase 'ERROR', while the message keywords match in any case. The inverse also exists — inside a globally IGNORECASE pattern, `(?-i:ERROR)` re-sensitizes one group. Two mechanical notes. Global flags like (?i) must appear at the very start of the pattern (or not at all): since Python 3.11, a bare (?i) in the middle is a compile error, not a warning — the scoped form is the supported way to switch flags mid-pattern. And scoped flags compose with VERBOSE layouts nicely, which matters because case rules are exactly the kind of intent a reader can't infer from the pattern text: `(?i:...)` says 'this part is case-insensitive on purpose' in a way a file-level re.I never can. Prefer the narrowest scope that expresses the rule — a global re.I on a pattern where only one group is case-free is how validators quietly start accepting 'error' as a level.

The one-big-regex approach earns its complexity when records genuinely span lines (a log entry with a stack trace attached), when you need matches that cross line boundaries, or when you're extracting scattered islands from unstructured text rather than parsing a record format. The $ in Python matches at the end OR just before a trailing newline (and, under MULTILINE, before every newline). The porting trap is that the naming is flipped relative to Perl and Ruby: THERE, \Z has the trailing-newline exception and \z is absolute; a pattern moved from Perl to Python that relied on \Z meaning 'end, forgiving one newline' silently becomes stricter, and one that used \z won't compile at all. In Python the safe habits are: fullmatch for validation (no anchor involved), \Z when you truly mean 'absolute end' inside a larger pattern, and $ only when the newline behavior is what you want — typically line-oriented searching under MULTILINE. If you're porting patterns between languages, anchors are the first thing to audit, before character classes: the $/\Z/\z triangle and the meaning of \d under Unicode account for a large share of 'same pattern, different result' bugs.

import re

TOKEN = re.compile(r'(?P<NUMBER>\d+(?:\.\d+)?)|(?P<OP>[+\-*/()])|(?P<SKIP>\s+)')


class Parser:
    def __init__(self, src):
        self.tokens = [(m.lastgroup, m.group()) for m in TOKEN.finditer(src)
                       if m.lastgroup != 'SKIP']
        self.pos = 0

    def peek(self):
        return self.tokens[self.pos][1] if self.pos < len(self.tokens) else None

    def eat(self, value=None):
        tok = self.tokens[self.pos]
        if value is not None and tok[1] != value:
            raise ValueError(f'expected {value}, got {tok[1]}')
        self.pos += 1
        return tok

    def expr(self):  # expr := term (('+'|'-') term)*
        value = self.term()
        while self.peek() in ('+', '-'):
            op = self.eat()[1]
            rhs = self.term()
            value = value + rhs if op == '+' else value - rhs
        return value

    def term(self):  # term := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
        value = self.factor()
        while self.peek() in ('*', '/'):
            op = self.eat()[1]
            rhs = self.factor()
            value = value * rhs if op == '*' else value / rhs
        return value

    def factor(self):  # factor := NUMBER | '(' expr ')'
        if self.peek() == '(':
            self.eat('(')
            value = self.expr()
            self.eat(')')
            return value
        return float(self.eat()[1])


for src in ['2 + 3 * 4', '(2 + 3) * 4', '10 / 4 - 1', '2 * (3 + 4) - 5']:
    print(src, '=', Parser(src).expr())

messages.content: This is recursive descent: one method per grammar rule, and the precedence falls out of the CALL STRUCTURE rather than a table. `expr` handles + and -, but it gets its operands from `term`; `term` handles * and /, getting operands from `factor`; `factor` is a number or a parenthesized `expr` — recursion, the thing regex can't do, is what makes parentheses free. So '2 + 3 * 4' is 14.0 because expr sees 2, then asks term for the right operand, and term consumes '3 * 4' as a unit before expr adds. '(2 + 3) * 4' is 20.0 because factor evaluates the parenthesized expr first. The results print as floats because factor converts numbers with float() and '/' is true division — a deliberate, visible choice. Compare the whole apparatus with the tokenizer before it: same TOKEN pattern, and the parser adds maybe forty lines. That's the rung above regex on the ladder — not a bigger pattern, a different kind of machine, one whose call stack is the memory regex doesn't have. And note what's absent: eval(), which would also 'work' and would also execute anything the input cared to smuggle in.

A quote toggles in_string only when escaped is false; a backslash sets escaped for exactly one character; collect characters while in_string. It handles every case by construction and reads like the rule it implements. There IS a famous regex contortion — `"(?:\\.|[^"\\])*"` — which handles backslash escapes by offering 'an escaped anything' as an alternative to 'a non-quote, non-backslash character'. It's correct for this one escape rule, and worth knowing. But watch what happens as the format grows: add raw strings, add multiline strings, add string prefixes, and each rule multiplies the pattern's alternatives while the state machine gains a branch. The pattern is a party trick that scales negatively; the state machine is the same idea written in a notation designed for state. Depth 3 needs a different memory than depth 300, and depth 300 than depth 300,000; a machine with N states can distinguish at most N different 'how deep am I' situations, so for any regex there is a depth at which it must confuse two situations and give a wrong answer. This is the pumping-lemma intuition, and it's a ceiling on the formalism, not on your cleverness. Two corollaries people get wrong. First, backreferences don't lift the ceiling for nesting — they let a pattern repeat captured TEXT, which buys other powers (matching 'the the'), but they don't provide a counter. Second, for any FIXED depth bound d, a regex technically exists — you can unroll the counting into the pattern — it's just astronomically large and useless, which is why 'regex can't parse nested structures' is the correct engineering shorthand. The parser's stack (or a single integer counter) is exactly the unbounded memory the formalism lacks; the moment a problem needs it, you've identified the right tool.

My log lines sometimes wrap — a stack trace continues on following lines that don't start with a timestamp. My line-by-line parser mangles these records. What's the standard move?

Split the problem into the two phases it actually has: RECORD FRAMING first, field parsing second. A new record begins at a line that starts with a timestamp (a cheap shape check — a pattern like `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T` or even a strptime attempt); any line that doesn't start a record is a CONTINUATION of the previous one and gets appended to its buffer, newlines preserved. Only when a buffer is complete — because the next header line arrived, or the file ended — do you run the field parser on it, stack trace and all, typically stashing the continuation text in a 'detail' field. Implemented as a generator, this is a dozen lines: keep a current buffer, yield it when a header line appears, start a fresh one. The mistake to avoid is trying to make ONE regex span the wrapping — a DOTALL pattern that swallows multi-line records will eventually swallow two records as one, because nothing in it knows where records end. Framing is a stateful, line-at-a-time decision ('does this line start something new?'), and stateful decisions belong in code around the pattern, not inside it.

Half my log sources emit plain text lines, half emit JSON lines. Should I route the JSON ones through my regex parser too, for consistency?

No — consistency belongs to the RECORDS, not the parsing mechanism. For JSON lines, json.loads per line is correct by construction: it handles key order, escaping, nesting, and numbers as numbers. A regex over JSON text gives you the usual failures — the first '"id"' in the text rather than the top-level one, values that change when the producer pretty-prints, string contents that look like fields. What SHOULD be consistent is the dict shape each source produces: write one small adapter per format (parse_text_line, parse_json_line), each returning {'ts': ..., 'svc': ..., 'level': ..., 'user': ...} with the same keys and the same None-for-absent convention. Then every downstream aggregate, alert, and report is format-blind and written once. The smell to watch for is the reverse: one parser per format AND one downstream per format, which doubles every future change. Adapters at the boundary, one record shape inside — that's the whole architecture.
After my regex extracts log timestamps as strings like '2026-11-26T14:03:11.042Z', how do I compute things like the gap between the first and last ERROR?

Convert at parse time, and never do arithmetic on the strings. The regex's job ends at shape: it guarantees the timestamp LOOKS like a timestamp. Then datetime.fromisoformat — in Python 3.11 and later it accepts the 'Z' suffix and fractional seconds directly — turns it into a real datetime, which goes into the record next to the other fields. From there the gap is just `last - first` on the ERROR records' datetimes, a timedelta you can compare, threshold, and format properly. The anti-pattern is string arithmetic: subtracting the seconds fields, comparing timestamps lexicographically across timezones, or slicing fixed-width pieces out of the string — each works on the sample and breaks on a format variant (a missing fraction, a +02:00 offset, a date rollover at midnight). Rule of thumb for the whole pipeline: text at the boundary, types inside. The moment a value needs math, ordering, or comparison, it should already be a datetime, an int, or a Decimal — parsed once, at the edge, by the tool that understands the format.
My log file is 4 GB. I currently read it all into one string and run findall over it. What's the streaming pattern?

Iterate the file object — a file is its own line iterator, so `for line in f:` never holds more than one line in memory. Parse each line into a record (or None), fold it into your running state, and let the line be discarded: Counters for levels and services, a running sum for bytes, a 'top errors' heap if you need rankings. Your memory use becomes proportional to the STATE (distinct keys in the counters), not to the file size — flat whether the file is 4 GB or 400 GB. Two refinements for when the state itself is the problem: if you only need some lines, filter BEFORE parsing (a cheap `if 'ERROR' not in line: continue` pre-filter, verified against your format, can skip 95% of the work); and if you need records rather than aggregates, write them out incrementally to the next stage instead of accumulating a list. findall over a whole-file string is fine for kilobyte inputs and code samples; the moment the input is a real log, the line loop with running aggregates is the professional default — it's also, not coincidentally, the shape that survives the file growing.

How do I know my log regex is DONE? It keeps growing a new optional group every week as new line shapes appear.

A growing pattern is a symptom, and the diagnosis matters more than the cure. Each new optional group means the FORMAT grew a variant. A few variants are normal — formats have optional fields. But weekly growth means one of two things: the producer keeps changing (a process problem — you need the format versioned or the variants enumerated with the team that emits them), or what you call one format is really TWO formats sharing a file (two services, an old and a new logger) and they deserve two adapters producing one record shape. The 'done' test is empirical: freeze a sample suite — a few dozen real lines covering every known variant plus junk — and require 100% accounted-for (parsed or explicitly skipped) before the pattern may change. When a new variant appears, its line goes into the suite FIRST, failing, and the pattern change is done when the whole suite passes again. That's the same pattern-library-with-tests discipline used for validators. If the suite keeps growing past a few dozen lines, stop and split the formats — a pattern with fifteen optional groups isn't a parser anymore, it's an archive of surprises, and it will start accepting lines that are none of the variants, just their recombination.

The librarian. The pattern checks the SHAPE of an ISBN-13 — starts with 978 or 979, thirteen digits — and 9780306406158 has a perfect shape. So ISBN validation is two layers: the pattern as a cheap gate (also good for routing: 'this isn't even ISBN-shaped, don't bother'), and ten lines of arithmetic as the actual validator. Any identifier with a check digit — ISBN, ISSN, IBAN, card numbers — has the same structure, and a shape-only validator for one is a bug that passes review.

What's the general principle behind the ISBN and date failures? I keep writing validators that pass review and fail in production.

Your validators fail because a regex can only state facts about CHARACTERS AT POSITIONS — 'position 3 is a digit', 'the string is 13 long'. Production validity usually involves three other kinds of fact that no pattern can hold. RELATIONS between parts: a check digit is a function of the other digits; February's length is a function of the month and year fields. RANGES tied to meaning: \d{2} accepts 99 as a month because 'two digits' and '01–12' are different claims, and only the first is a character claim. EXISTENCE in the world: whether this ISBN was ever issued, whether this account exists, whether this domain receives mail — no string inspection can answer those at all. So validation is a stack of layers, one per kind of fact: shape (regex's layer, and it's a good one — cheap, total, and it makes the later layers' input sane), then range and checksum checks in code, then semantic and existence checks against the system of record. Review fails to catch the problem because a pattern LOOKS like a complete validator. The fix in review is one question: 'which layer is this, and what do the other layers look like?' If the answer is 'this is all of it', you've found the bug before production does.

The maintainable cure is usually not the giant official regex: split the string on '.' and '+'/'-' boundaries in code, check each component with a tiny rule (all digits, no leading zero), and keep a named is_valid_semver function whose tests quote the spec. A pattern is a fine first gate ('three numeric-ish parts'); the spec's edge rules belong in code where they can be individually tested and individually read.

Allowlist or denylist for input validation — which side should I err on?

Allowlist, and it isn't close. An allowlist states what IS accepted ('ASCII letters, digits, hyphen, underscore; 1–64 chars; not exactly . or ..') and everything unlisted fails by default — it fails CLOSED, including against attacks and edge cases nobody has thought of yet. A denylist states what is FORBIDDEN ('no .., no /, no backslash, no null byte...') and everything unlisted passes — it fails OPEN against the first encoding trick, Unicode lookalike, or separator variant you didn't enumerate. The history of input-validation bugs is largely a history of denylists meeting an unlisted case. Denylists still have two legitimate jobs: as a SECOND layer that produces better error messages ('that name is reserved' is friendlier than 'invalid'), and for the small set of things that are specifically dangerous in context even inside an otherwise valid value (a leading '-' that a downstream CLI will read as a flag). But the security decision — accept or reject — should be made by the allowlist. Practical corollary: when you review a validator, ask 'what does this ACCEPT?' and try to get the author to say it in one sentence. If they can only tell you what it blocks, you've found the problem.
My cron-expression validator just checks the five-field shape with a pattern. A user entered '61 * * * *' and it passed validation, then the scheduler choked. What's the missing layer?

Ranges — the same missing layer as the date pattern. '61' is a perfectly good two-digit number; it's just not a minute. Cron fields have per-field bounds (minute 0–59, hour 0–23, day-of-month 1–31, month 1–12, day-of-week 0–7) and per-field vocabularies (JAN, MON), plus structural elements a shape pattern barely touches: lists ('1,15,30'), ranges ('9-17'), steps ('*/15'), and combinations of all three in one field. None of those facts are character facts. The sane architecture mirrors dates exactly: a light pattern (or a split on whitespace) to establish 'five fields of plausible characters', then a per-field parser in code that expands lists/ranges/steps and range-checks every resulting number against that field's bounds — which has the side benefit of producing precise errors ('minute 61 out of range') instead of the scheduler's choke. If your platform has a cron library, prefer it for the same reason you'd use a date parser: the bounds and vocabularies are a specification someone else already maintains. Shape first, semantics second, and never let the shape layer sign off alone.
Pull it together for me: I'm building the signup-form validator for email addresses. What should the regex layer do, and what must it never be trusted with?

Give the regex layer a small, honest job: a coarse filter that rejects obvious garbage before anything expensive happens. One '@', a non-empty local part and domain, no whitespace, a dot somewhere in the domain, and length caps (the RFC limits — 64 for the local part, 254 overall — are among the few hard facts available). Something like `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$` plus length checks is the right size. Now the never-trust list. Never trust it with DELIVERABILITY: a perfectly shaped address can belong to no mailbox on Earth; the only true validation of an email address is sending a confirmation message to it, which is why serious signups are built around the confirmation loop, not around a cleverer pattern. Never trust it with the RFC's full grammar: quoted local parts ('"weird @ local"@example.com') are legal, and a pattern strict enough to reject them will eventually reject a real user, while a pattern loose enough to accept everything legal accepts everything, period. And never trust it with POLICY — disposable domains, role addresses, your own blocklists — which are business rules that live in code and data, change weekly, and have no business being compiled into a pattern. The pattern is the bouncer checking that you have a ticket-shaped object; the confirmation email is the turnstile. Systems that ask the bouncer to be the turnstile end up either turning away customers or waving through bots, and usually both.
I split a sentence with re.split and my punctuation vanished. A coworker says 'put a group around the separator'. Why does that bring the separators back?

Because re.split has a documented dual behavior. With a plain pattern, the matched separators are delimiters and are discarded: re.split(r'[.!?]', 'Hi. Bye!') gives ['Hi', ' Bye', '']. Wrap the separator in a capturing group — re.split(r'([.!?])', 'Hi. Bye!') — and the separators are INCLUDED in the result: ['Hi', '.', ' Bye', '!', '']. The rationale is exactly your use case: sometimes the delimiter is data (punctuation for a tokenizer, operators in an expression, the quotes around fields) and you need it in the stream to reconstruct or interpret the pieces. Two practical notes. The pieces now alternate content/separator/content, so consumers should expect that rhythm — including possible empty strings at the ends when the text starts or ends with a separator. And if your separator pattern contains a group that can fail to participate (an optional branch), you'll get None entries in the list where that group sat out — use non-capturing groups for any structure inside the separator that isn't itself meant to be returned. Knowing this one behavior turns re.split from a blunt splitter into a light tokenizer.

What's re.Scanner? I've never seen it used in real code.

It's the stdlib's little-known built-in lexer. You construct it with a list of (pattern, callback) pairs; scan(string) walks the string trying the patterns in order at each position, calls the matching pattern's callback with the match, and collects the callbacks' return values as tokens. It returns a pair: the token list and the UNMATCHED REMAINDER — that second element is its most honest feature, since it forces you to confront the input your patterns couldn't cover instead of silently skipping it. Why you've never seen it: a hand-rolled finditer loop over one alternation of named groups (the tokenizer shape) does the same job with the patterns in one visible place, better error positions, and no extra API to learn — so the ecosystem standardized on that instead. Scanner still earns a mention for quick one-off lexers and for its remainder-reporting discipline: whatever tokenizer you write, steal that part. A lexer that reports what it couldn't consume will save you from the silent-token-loss bugs that plague the ones that can't.
Does re.compile actually matter, or is it cargo cult? The module-level functions take pattern strings fine.

Mostly it matters less than the folklore says — with one sharp exception. The re module caches compiled patterns (the cache holds 512 entries), so calling re.search(r'\d+', s) in a loop does NOT recompile every time; the string is looked up and the compiled object reused. For literal patterns in ordinary code, compile is documentation, not performance: a named module-level `DATE_RE = re.compile(...)` tells readers the pattern is a fixed, shared contract, and it gives you one place to change it. The exception is DYNAMIC patterns — built from variables, f-strings, user input, per-tenant configuration. Those miss the cache constantly, can thrash it for everyone else, and are exactly where you should compile once, deliberately, and hold the object. Compiled patterns also unlock the method forms with extras the module functions don't expose as conveniently — Pattern.fullmatch, and search/match with pos/endpos for resumption scanning. So: cargo cult if someone claims raw speed for literals; genuinely important for dynamic patterns, for API clarity, and for treating a pattern as a named, testable artifact rather than a string repeated at call sites.

I need match POSITIONS, not just matched text — I'm building a highlighter that marks every measurement like '41s' or '2.5kg' in a document. findall only gives me strings.

finditer is the tool: it yields match objects, and each match carries .span() — the (start, end) offsets of the whole match — plus .start(group) / .end(group) if you need a subgroup's position. Your highlighter becomes: compile something like `\d+(?:\.\d+)?\s?(?:kg|s|ms|cm)`, iterate finditer over the document, and collect the spans into whatever your renderer consumes (annotation offsets, HTML <mark> insertion points, editor decorations). findall can't do this job at all — it discards positions by design, returning only text (or tuples), which is fine for extraction and useless for annotation. Two working notes. Spans refer to the string you searched; if you transform the document, recompute them rather than adjusting by hand. And when you need to ACT on the spans — wrapping matches in markup, say — process them from the END of the document backwards, or build the output by splicing left to right from the original string, so earlier insertions don't shift the offsets of later matches. Positions are a different product than text; the moment a feature needs them, you're in finditer territory permanently.
Give me the house rules for regex readability you'd put in a team style guide.

Six rules, all earned the hard way by somebody. One pattern, one job: a pattern that extracts AND validates AND normalizes will do all three badly — split the jobs. Named groups always, once a pattern has more than two groups: the names are documentation that can't drift from the code, and they make groupdict() possible downstream. VERBOSE mode when the pattern needs a comment — if you have to explain it, lay it out and explain it inline, remembering to escape literal spaces and hashes. Any pattern longer than roughly one line gets a test table (should-match / shouldn't-match rows) in the same commit; an untested long pattern is a rumor. Never grow a pattern by appending alternation branches for exceptions — the third 'or also handle...' branch is the format telling you it has variants that want separate patterns or a parser. And keep patterns in one named place (a patterns module), compiled once: the same regex typed at five call sites is five regexes waiting to disagree. Underlying all six: a regex is code that other people must review at reading speed. If it can't be reviewed, it doesn't matter that it works — today.
I'm parsing a long string of successive key=value pairs and want to resume scanning where the last match ended, instead of findall's all-at-once. Is there a way?

Yes — the compiled pattern's methods take pos: `pat.search(s, pos)` starts searching at index pos, and `pat.match(s, pos)` tries to match exactly AT pos. The resumption loop is: match at the cursor, process the pair, set the cursor to m.end(), repeat — with match() rather than search() you also get gap detection for free, because a failed match at the cursor means 'the next thing here is not a pair' instead of findall's silent skip to the next pair somewhere downstream. Two semantic warnings. pos is a search offset, not a new string: ^ and \A still refer to the REAL start of the string (under MULTILINE, ^ also matches after newlines as usual), so resumption patterns should be written without ^ anchors — anchor with the match-at-cursor discipline instead. And endpos exists too, for treating a slice as the world without copying it. When is this worth it over finditer, which already walks matches left to right? When your consumption is conditional — stop early, back off on errors, interleave parsing with other logic — the explicit cursor puts you in control of advancement, which is the first step from 'scanning' toward 'parsing'.
My app lets users supply their own search regex. A malformed pattern crashes the request with re.error. How should user-supplied patterns be handled?

Treat a user-supplied pattern as untrusted input in two distinct ways. First, validity: compile inside try/except re.error and turn the exception into a 400-style response carrying the error message — re.error messages even include a position ('missing ), unterminated subpattern at position 0'), which makes a genuinely helpful error to show the user. Never let it bubble into a 500; a typo'd pattern is a client error, full stop. Second, and easier to miss: a VALID user pattern is a denial-of-service surface. The user controls both the pattern and, often, the text — a nested-quantifier pattern over a long document is a ReDoS the user can trigger against your workers at will. Defenses: cap pattern length and input length; run matches under a timeout (the third-party regex module's timeout= argument, or a worker with a deadline); or — the option most products should pick — don't offer raw regex at all. Offer the safe subset users actually want: plain substring, prefix, or glob-style wildcards, translated by YOU into safe patterns. Full regex as a user feature is a power tool; products that ship it inherit the support burden of every backtracking seminar ever given.

The empty-sep case is equally useful: if sep comes back '', the line had no '=' at all — malformed input detected with no pattern and no exception handling. partition is the right size of tool when the structure is 'one separator, two sides'. The regex earns its keep when the situation grows teeth: pairs embedded in free text, values with shapes to validate, multiple separators with different roles. The senior dev's real point isn't about this line — it's that reaching for regex FIRST skips the question 'what's the simplest mechanism that expresses this structure?', and string methods are simpler: no pattern language, no escaping, no review burden. Ask the question in that order and regex becomes the answer exactly when it should be.

Where does plain str.split() break down on real-world text? I keep reaching for it first — should I?

Reaching for it first is right; knowing its four walls is the skill. Wall one: quoted segments — the moment a field can contain the delimiter inside quotes ('Winter Park', 'Smith, John'), split shreds it, and no argument to split fixes that. Wall two: mixed and meaningful whitespace — split(None) handles runs of whitespace gracefully, but if columns are aligned by spaces (fixed-width reports), the spaces ARE the structure and splitting destroys the very thing that encodes the fields; those want slicing by column positions. Wall three: multi-character delimiters that can also appear inside values — split will cut on every occurrence, including the ones that were data. Wall four: structure in the pieces themselves — if after splitting you immediately run a regex on every piece, the split wasn't the parse, it was a pre-pass, and often the pattern should have owned the whole job. Notice none of these say 'split is bad': for whitespace-separated tokens, simple delimiters, and first-pass exploration it's the correct, fastest, clearest tool. The walls are where formats keep their secrets — quotes, escapes, alignment, nesting — and each wall is a signpost to the next rung up.
Give me the ladder: when I face a text problem, in what order should I try tools?

Five rungs, each justified by a failure of the one below. Rung 1, exact string methods — startswith, endswith, in, partition, strip, replace: if the structure is 'a fixed separator' or 'a fixed prefix', stop here; most text chores live here. Rung 2, split and join: token streams with a simple delimiter and no quoting. Rung 3, regex: flat patterns — field extraction, shape validation, islands in prose — anywhere the pieces don't nest and delimiters can't hide inside values. Rung 4, a hand state machine or counter: escapes, quoted strings, balanced delimiters, record framing — the problems whose rule is 'remember one thing while scanning'. Rung 5, a real parser or library: the format has a specification and a maintainer — csv, json, html.parser, ast — or a genuine grammar, where recursive descent or a parser generator earns its keep. Two rules for using the ladder: start at the lowest rung that could POSSIBLY work, because lower tools are simpler, faster, and easier to review; and when a tool fails, name the specific structural feature that defeated it (nesting? escapes? a spec?) — that feature, not frustration, tells you which rung to climb to. Skipping rungs wastes effort; refusing to climb wastes more.
Remove /* ... */ comments from C-like code, including the nasty case: '/* outer /* inner */ still comment */'. My regex removed up to the first */ and left 'still comment */' as code. Handled how?

Start with a plot twist: in actual C, your regex was RIGHT. C comments do not nest — the first */ ends the comment, and 'still comment */' really is (broken) code in C; the 'nasty case' is a syntax error in the source, not a parser challenge. Which produces the first lesson: before escalating tools, check the format's ACTUAL rules — some formats that look nestable aren't, and some that look flat aren't (C++ raw strings, SQL block comments in some dialects DO nest). Now suppose your format genuinely nests comments — some languages' do. Then no regex can do it, for the balanced-parentheses reason: finding the */ that matches a given /* requires counting depth. The tool is the familiar counter loop: scan for /* and */ tokens, depth++ on open, depth-- on close, drop everything while depth > 0. Fifteen lines, obviously correct, and it degrades gracefully — an unterminated comment shows up as 'depth 1 at end of input', an error you can report with a position, where the regex version would have silently produced something. Match the tool to the format's real grammar, not to the grammar you assumed it had.
My config file contains Python literals: {'retries': 3, 'hosts': ['a', 'b'], 'debug': True}. I started writing a parser for it. Stop me if there's a library.

Stop. ast.literal_eval exists for exactly this: it parses a Python literal — strings, numbers, tuples, lists, dicts, booleans, None, nested arbitrarily — and returns the object, without executing anything. It's the safe sibling of eval (which you must never point at config files, since eval runs arbitrary code; literal_eval accepts only literal structure and rejects names, calls, and operators beyond numeric signs). Your hand parser would have spent its first hour on strings with escapes and its second on nested lists, reinventing a grammar that already has a maintained implementation. The general principle is the top rung of the ladder: when the text IS a known format — a Python literal, JSON, CSV, TOML (tomllib), YAML (with a safe loader) — the library is not a shortcut, it's the specification, kept correct by people who read the edge cases so you don't have to. Write parsers for YOUR formats, the ones nobody else has specified. For everyone else's formats, your job is choosing the right library and validating the RESULT (is 'retries' present? is it an int?) — which is where your code's actual value lives.
A teammate wants to generate a full parser with a parser generator for splitting our log timestamps. When is that overkill?

When the 'grammar' fits in one sentence and never changes. A timestamp is a fixed-shape token: a pattern or even a strptime format string describes it completely, and a parser generator buys you a grammar file, a generation step in the build, a runtime dependency, and parse errors phrased in the generator's vocabulary — all to split '2026-11-26T14:03:11' into fields. The costs are real and recurring; the benefit is zero, because there is no grammar to speak of: no recursion, no precedence, no ambiguity. Parser generators pay off in the opposite country: a real language or protocol with productions that interact — expressions with precedence, nested structures, a specification that will grow new constructs over years, and error recovery requirements. There, hand-rolling is the false economy. The decision heuristic is the ladder question again: does the structure nest, recurse, or evolve? A timestamp does none of the three. There's also a social cost worth naming: every generated parser in a codebase is a subsystem only its author can debug at 3 a.m. Spend that capital where the grammar is genuinely earning it, and let timestamps be a one-liner the whole team can read.
Log line: '2026-11-26 14:03:11 ERROR auth login failed for user ana'. I want date, time, level, service, and the REST as one message string. Regex feels heavy for this.

It is — the forgotten middle rung is split with maxsplit: `line.split(None, 4)` splits on runs of whitespace at most four times and returns five pieces, the last being the entire remainder, spaces intact: ['2026-11-26', '14:03:11', 'ERROR', 'auth', 'login failed for user ana']. No pattern, no groups, and the message keeps its internal spacing because splitting simply stops. maxsplit is the right tool whenever the format is 'a few fixed fields, then free text' — log lines, command histories, simple headers — a shape that occurs constantly and that people routinely over-solve with a five-group pattern. Its limits are the usual ones: fields must be whitespace-separated with no quoting (a service named 'auth service' would break it), and it validates nothing — if you need to CHECK that field one is really a date, that's a separate step on the pieces. But as pure dissection, split(None, n) is faster to write, faster to read, and harder to get wrong than the equivalent regex. Keep it next to partition in the 'try before regex' drawer.
In code review, what questions tell me which rung of the text-parsing ladder a problem sits on?

Three questions, asked in order, settle most reviews. First: 'Can pieces nest, quote, or escape each other?' If a value can contain the delimiter, or a structure can contain itself, you're at the state-machine/parser rungs no matter how flat the sample data looks — demand the sample that nests, because production will supply it. Second: 'Is there a maintained parser for this exact format?' If the text is CSV, JSON, HTML, a Python literal, a URL — the review is over; the only acceptable diff calls the library and validates the result. Third: 'What do we need FROM the text — pieces, positions, or a structure?' Pieces suggest split/findall; positions demand finditer spans; a structure (a tree, an evaluation, a record with relationships) means a parser, and any regex in the diff is a lexer at best. A useful fourth, when the first three don't decide it: 'When this format grows — and it will — which tool makes the growth a one-line change?' The pattern that needs a new alternation branch per variant, or the parser that needs a new rule: pick the one whose growth path you can describe. Reviewers who ask these four questions catch the 'regex for HTML' class of bug at the only cheap moment — before it's written.

Capstone: parse this small access log properly. Lines have fixed head fields, a bracketed timestamp, a quoted request with spaces inside it, then status and size, then two more quoted fields (referrer, user agent) that I don't need. Use the right tool per part and give me per-line fields, status counts, and total bytes.

arguments.code:
import re
from collections import Counter

LOG = '''10.0.0.8 - - [26/Nov/2026:14:03:11] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)"
10.0.0.9 - - [26/Nov/2026:14:03:12] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 302 128 "https://example.com/" "curl/8.0"
10.0.0.8 - - [26/Nov/2026:14:03:15] "GET /missing HTTP/1.1" 404 64 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)"'''

# split() takes the fixed head fields; the regex takes the bracketed and
# quoted request; the trailing quoted fields (referrer, agent) contain
# spaces and are deliberately skipped, not parsed.
head = re.compile(r'(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<when>[^\]]+)\] '
                  r'"(?P<method>\w+) (?P<path>\S+) [^"]*" '
                  r'(?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\d+)')
rows = [m.groupdict() for m in head.finditer(LOG)]
for r in rows:
    print(r['ip'], r['method'], r['path'], r['status'], r['size'])
print('statuses   :', dict(Counter(r['status'] for r in rows)))
print('total bytes:', sum(int(r['size']) for r in rows))

messages.content: The parse is a study in not parsing. The head fields are fixed-position and space-separated — the pattern takes them as \S+ runs without ceremony. The bracketed timestamp is captured as 'everything up to ]' — a negated class, not a date grammar, because nothing here needs to compute with it. The quoted request is the interesting field: it contains spaces, so whitespace logic dies there, but the pattern only needs method and path from inside the quotes and lets `[^\"]*` skip the rest ('HTTP/1.1'). And the two trailing quoted fields — referrer and user agent, the ones with parentheses and semicolons and every delimiter you'd hate — are not parsed AT ALL: the pattern ends at the size field, because the questions (fields, status counts, total bytes) never touch them. Parsing data you don't need is how parsers break on data you don't control. Results: three rows extracted cleanly, one each of 200/302/404, total bytes 704. Every field got the cheapest tool that is CORRECT for it — split-level simplicity where the format is fixed, a class where a delimiter is reliable, and deliberate ignorance where the format is hostile and the data is unneeded. That triage, done consciously per field, is the entire discipline of this batch in one example.
